name: Sandbox
body:
Describe the new page here.
Samajh gaya bhai, tumhe shortcut nahi chahiye. Har kaam ke baad foran baad kya karna hai chahiye, 5-5 min ka breakdown. 

Tumhare timing pe based ye hai full minute-by-minute chart. Isse print karke laga do:

📋 *Minute-by-Minute Routine Chart - School Day*

Sleep: 10:00 PM | Wake: 6:00 AM*

Time	Kaam	Foran Baad Kya Karna Hai

6:00 - 6:05 AM**	Utho, bed chhodo	1 glass lukewarm pani piyo
6:05 - 6:10 AM**	5 min stretch + deep breathing	Bathroom jao
6:10 - 6:20 AM**	Fresh ho jao, brush, munh dho	1 glass normal pani piyo
6:20 - 6:35 AM**	Nashta karo	Bag check karo, bottle bharo
6:35 - 6:55 AM**	Kapde, shoes, last prep	Ghar se niklo
6:55 - 7:00 AM**	School pahucho	Class me beth jao
7:00 AM - 2:00 PM**	School	Har 1 ghante me 2-3 ghont pani piyo
2:00 - 2:10 PM**	Ghar aao, kapde badlo	Haath-munh dho
2:10 - 2:25 PM**	Khana khao	5 min walk karo
2:25 - 2:30 PM**	Bed ready karo	Sone ke liye beth jao
2:30 - 2:50 PM**	20 min power nap	Uthte hi 1 glass pani piyo
2:50 - 3:00 PM**	Bag ready karo, nikalne ki tayyari	Tuition ke liye niklo
3:00 - 6:00 PM**	Tuition	Paani saath rakho
6:00 - 6:10 PM**	Ghar aao	Shoes utaro, fresh ho jao
6:10 - 6:20 PM**	Halka nashta + lassi/lemon water	10 min slow walk karo
6:20 - 6:30 PM**	Rest karo	Mobile/tablet on karo
6:30 - 7:30 PM**	Free Time / Mobile-Game	1 ghanta khatam hote hi band karo
7:30 - 7:40 PM**	Mobile side rakho, table pe betho	Homework copy nikalo
7:40 - 8:30 PM**	Homework karo	5 min break lo
8:30 - 8:40 PM**	Haath dho, dinner ke liye betho	Dinner khao
8:40 - 9:30 PM**	Dinner + family time	Table saaf karo
9:30 - 9:40 PM**	Kal ka uniform, bag ready karo	Revision copy nikalo
9:40 - 9:55 PM**	Halki revision / next day dekho	Phone door rakho
9:55 - 10:00 PM**	Bed pe jao, light off karo	So jao
10:00 PM**	Sleep	6:00 AM utho

---

🔑 *Important Choti Choti Baatein*
1. *Pani*: School me 4-5 glass, ghar pe 4-5 glass. Ek saath mat piyo.
2. *Garmi ka tip*: Bottle me choti choti cheeni + namak daal do. Weakness nahi hogi.
3. *Nap skip mat karna*: 20 min ki neend se tuition me neend nahi aayegi.
4. *7:30 PM ke baad phone door*: Agar nahi rakha to poora schedule kharab ho jayega.

---

Ye follow karo 21 din. Har kaam ke baad agla step likha hua hai, isliye confuse nahi hoge.

Chaho to main iska *Sunday wala relaxed version* bhi isi format me bana dun jisme training aur free time zyada ho. Banau?

 Platform:  Plan 9 from Bell Labs
 License:   Open source
 Screenshot:

The primary text editor on the Plan9FromBellLabs operating system.

In the words of Eric S. Raymond:

 Sam is a fairly straightforward descendant of ed, remaining much closer to its parent than vi. Sam incorporates only two new concepts: a curses-style text display and text selection with the mouse.  [...]  Because the mouse is available to do selections and rapidly change focus between buffers (including the command buffer), Sam needs no equivalent of the default (command) mode of vi. The hundreds of extended vi commands are unnecessary and, therefore, omitted. Overall, Sam adds only about a dozen commands to the seventeen or so in the ed set, for a total of about thirty. [1]

In addition, the internals to Sam are quite interesting too since it is implemented as a two part editor. Of course, the concept of Plumbing is pretty unique to Plan9FromBellLabs.

There is a version for Windows that allows you to get a feel for this innovative TextEditor.

There was an interview October 18th, 2004 on http://SlashDot.org with Rob Pike (author of sam) who was asked:

 Emacs or Vi? - by Neil Blender

 Pike:

 Neither.

 When I was a lad, I hacked up the 6th Edition ed with Tom Duff, Hugh Redelmeier, and David Tilbrook to resuscitate qed, the editor Ken Thompson wrote for CTSS that was the inspiration for the much slimmer ed. (Children must learn these things for themselves.) Dennis Ritchie has a nice history of qed at http://cm.bell-labs.com/cm/cs/who/dmr/qed.html

 I liked qed for one key reason: it was really good at editing a number of files simultaneously. Ed only handled one file at a time.

 Ed and qed were command-driven line editors designed for printing terminals, not full-screen displays.  After I got to Bell Labs, I tried out VI but it could only handle one file at a time, which I found too limiting. Then I tried emacs, which handled multiple files but much more clumsily than qed. But the thing that bothered me most about vi and emacs was that they gave you a two-dimensional display of your file but you had only a one-dimensional input device to talk to them. It was like giving directions with a map on the table, but being forced to say "up a little, right, no back down, right there, yes turn there that's the spot" instead of just putting your finger on the map.

 (Today, emacs and vi support the mouse, but back in 1980 the versions I had access to had no support for mice. For that matter, there weren't really many mice yet.)

 So as soon as the Blit started to work, it was time to write an editor that used the mouse as an input device. I used qed (mostly) and emacs (a little) to write the first draft of jim, a full-screen editor that showed you text you could point to with a mouse. Jim handled multiple files very smoothly, and was really easy to use, but it was not terribly powerful. (Similar editors had been at Xerox PARC and other research labs but, well, children must learn these things for themselves.)

 A few years later I took the basic input idea of jim and put a new ed-like command language underneath it and called it sam, a locally popular editor that still has its adherents today. To me, the proof of sam's success was that it was the first full screen editor Ken Thompson liked. (He's still using it.) Here's the SP&E paper about sam from 1987: http://doc.cat-v.org/plan_9/4th_edition/papers/sam/

 A few years later, I decided the pop-up menu model for commanding an editor with a mouse was too restrictive, so I started over and built the much more radical ACME, which I'm using to write these answers. Here's the ACME paper: http://doc.cat-v.org/plan_9/4th_edition/papers/acme/

 I don't expect any Slashdot readers to switch editors after reading these papers (although the code is available for most major platforms), but I think it's worth reading about them to see that there are ways of editing - and working - that span a much larger gamut than is captured by the question, 'Emacs or VI?' 

 In an interview BrianKernighan said that his prefered editor is Sam and as second VI here is the link https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EF2-vcp1Te0

In the 1970s RCA lost over 1/2 a billion dollars trying (and failing) to compete with IBM in the mainframe computer market. They sold their computer system division to Sperry Univac (later Unisys) which included their Spctra 70 manframe with TSOS operating system. EDT was part of the supplied software. Since operating systems then were not considered something sold separately, it is possible that Ahmdahl Corporation (maker of IBM compatible mainframes, and later absorbed into Fujitsu) obtained a copy of the TSOS operating system which would have included EDT. (Univac made changes to the TSOS operating ssystem,renaming it VS/9, and the Spectra, adding virtual memory hardware as the Univac 90/60 (and later 90/70) mainframe.

EDT (BS2000/OSD)
User-friendly BS2000/OSD file editor for SAM (plain text) and ISAM files (text file with an index key for each line (or record) , allowing random access to any line in the file) text-type library elements and POSIX files.
Current version: V17.0

EDT is the user-friendly BS2000/OSD file editor for creating and editing standard BS2000 SAM and ISAM files, as well as text-type library elements and POSIX files.
It is used either in line or page mode. In line mode, you enter text or an editor command on a line, and press the transmit key. In page mode, you can use the cursor keys to move anywhere on the screen, making additions or deletions of text as you see fit. A line could be blanked out but could not be deleted, and new lines could not be added, until the transmit key was pressed, potentially including editor commands on a line by itself. Text on a line is distinguished from a command by starting with a single at (@) character as the first non-blank on a line. The @ command can be redefined to a different character, and to create a line beginning with @, two at symbols are used. The first @ symbol is stripped and the remainder of the line is considered a line of text.

It provides powerful yet easy-to-learn statements for performing frequently recurring operations (e.g. deleting, updating, inserting or copying records or characters, searching for records containing specific character strings, outputting records, etc.).

Benefits

 EDT is the foremost BS2000/OSD editor.
 It is a user-friendly full-screen editor for interactive applications and a powerful file editor for processing bulk data in batch mode. It thus fulfils practically all the requirements made of a modern file editor.
 EDT supports the PLAM access method. PLAM (Program Library Access Method) enables EDT to process library elements. Moreover, users who do not wish to utilize the full functionality of LMS can also process their programs in PLAM libraries.
 Support of UNICODE: This includes amongst others the possibility to handle differentially coded files in miscellaneous working files of EDT at the same time as well as the abolition of the limitation of record length (up to now 256 character). 
 It supports the equivalent of plug-ins through the @RUN command; if the program run via @RUN is EDT aware, it can access the in-memory editor buffer and use the file in memory. On the Univac VS/9 operating system, the @RUN command was used to execute the Waterloo Fortran Compiler, which essentially provided the equivalent of a Rapid Prototyping Tool on mainframe computers. 

'Other platforms'
EDT is also available for UNIX / Linux / MS-Windows from http://opg.de/produkte/index.html

Turbo Prolog was a highly optimized and statically typed version of the Prolog logic programming language. Marketed by Borland in the late 1980s, it brought an integrated development environment (IDE) and fast machine-code compilation to MS-DOS PCs, though it departed significantly from standard Edinburgh Prolog by requiring strict data typing. This is an implementation of and development environment for the descriptive programming language Prolog, it differs significantly from other implementations due to its strong data typing and influence from the Pascal language. It was released by Borland in 1988 for DOS. It has evolved into Visual Prolog, marketed and supported by PDC A/S.
